Our tale begins in 1998,  with Urza’s Saga bringing all sorts of horrendous   bullshit to the world, and also a gift—the cycling  mechanic. It’s a beautifully simple mechanic: you   can pay an alternate cost on a card and discard  it in order to draw a card. This began in simple   fashion during Urza Block, but five years later  Onslaught block added a ton of dimension to the   mechanic. Varied cycle costs, triggers attached  to cycle abilities, cycling for basic land types,   and six cards with triggered abilities when  other cards were cycled. These six were varying   power levels, with one in particular being just…  excellent, but we’ll talk about that a bit later. Cycling has seen additional prints every  few years since, and for a simple reason:   people like this mechanic. As an alternate cost  ability it adds a lot of flexibility to cards,   which leads to interesting decisionmaking. outro_45s: good idea on paper might make your deck make  a turn that isn’t what you were looking for. If I was to wrap this up in a bow, I’d go  with this: when you’re building a deck,   figure out what the deck wants to do, and try to  turn that into a somewhat focused plan. Accept   that you won’t nail the first version of the  deck, and that there’s room to adapt as you   encounter further problems. I’d say there  are four key versions of any single deck:   the first principles version in your brain,  the draft version after you actually hammer   out a 100 card list, the streamlined version  completed after you solo playtest a bit,   and the “final” version completed after you  play it against other people for a while.   Each of these steps will solve a different set of  problems that the deck has, and that’s a strength.

hook_60s: I am a hipster. I am an honest-to-god, dyed-in-the-wool EDH hipster. I like to play weird, unusual decks that do weird, unusual things with weird, unusual cards. The idea that I might be playing a deck that does something nobody has done before is extremely cool to me. And that specific task is something that is far more possible to do in EDH than in just about any other format. The format has a card selection that's almost as wide as Vintage is. It has thousands of different options for commanders. And the fact that it doesn't have a single set power level means that no deck is fully squeezed out as long as you're willing to shop around for an appropriate table to play at. The level of freedom that the format offers to deck builders can be genuinely overwhelming for the people who aren't used to that. outro_45s: as a way to inject variety and creativity into a game whose constructed formats were already rigid and meta-driven, even in the first few years of the game. Singleton meant being forced to play with underutilized cards. A wide card pool meant that decks could be constructed with basically any old cards sitting around, and a higher life total meant more space for creative but slower strategies that would likely get squeezed out by faster decks in a 20 health format. An Elder Dragon at the head of things gave an undeniable symbolic core to decks. Well, it wasn't exactly a replacement. The original deck is still fully playable, but I made a 10-card swap-out package that could be implemented to move the deck down from a cutthroat high-power combo deck that usually wins on turn five to a grandier pirate mid-range deck that usually wins on more like turn eight to 10. On the surface, that sounds fine, great even. I have a deck whose core I like and I get to split it into a high-powered bracket four style version and a more mid-powered three style version. However, the resulting theoretically mid-powered deck feels very strange to play and I think it points to some odd truths about what it means for a deck to be a particular power level. Something that might have already caught your attention is that 10 card number. A firmly bracket four deck is really just 10 cards from being a totally fair bracket three deck?
